title: The "data" URL scheme
summary: Defines the data URL scheme, which lets a small piece of data be placed directly inside a URL instead of being fetched from elsewhere. This is handy for embedding small images or text in a page. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A data URL carries its own small piece of content, such as a short note or a tiny image, instead of pointing to somewhere else. It works only for small things.

questions: how do i embed an image in a url
what is the data uri scheme
subtitle: A URL scheme that puts a small piece of data directly inside the URL itself.

tldr.problem: Some applications that use URLs need to embed small media type data inline, instead of pointing at something stored elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: The data scheme has the form data:[mediatype][;base64],data. The data is either base64 encoded or written with %xx escapes, and the media type defaults to text/plain;charset=US-ASCII.
tldr.outcome: The scheme is useful only for short values, since some applications limit URL length, and it makes it hard for firewalls to screen out risky media types.

today: RFC 2397 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Immediate Data in a URL
sections.content:
RFC 2397 defines a new URL scheme, data. It works like 'immediate addressing': a small data item is included in the URL as if it had been included externally.

The scheme is only useful for short values. Some applications limit URL length; for example, URLs inside HTML anchor tags are limited by the SGML declaration for HTML (RFC 1866), with LITLEN set at 1024. The scheme has no relative URL forms.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a web address tells a program where to go and fetch something. A data URL instead carries the small thing itself, so there is nothing left to fetch.

sections.title: Format and Encoding
sections.content:
A data URL looks like data:[<mediatype>][;base64],<data>. The media type is an Internet media type with optional parameters. If it is omitted, it defaults to text/plain;charset=US-ASCII, and text/plain may be left out while a charset parameter is supplied.

If ;base64 appears, the data is base64 encoded. Without it, safe URL characters are written as ASCII and other octets use the standard %xx hex escape. The ;base64 marker is told apart from a parameter because it has no following =. Parameter values should use URL escaping rather than quoted strings if they contain any tspecial, since the quote mark is itself not a valid URL character.
sections.plainLanguage: After the word data and a colon, you can say what kind of content it is, then a comma, then the content itself. A small marker says whether the content is encoded in a compact form.

sections.title: Examples and Uses
sections.content:
data:,A%20brief%20note encodes the text/plain string 'A brief note', which might be useful in a footnote link. A base64 GIF can be placed in an image tag's source for a small inline picture, though the RFC says that image is probably near the limit of utility and that anything larger is likely unsuitable.

A media type can include other parameters, as in data:text/plain;charset=iso-8859-7,%be%fg%be for a short sequence of Greek characters. The scheme can also pass setup parameters to a helper application for a particular media type. The RFC's history section notes that the idea was first proposed in August 1995 and that the scheme was already used in VRML, some new HTML applications, and commercial products.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hide a short note or a tiny picture right inside the address. The idea was already in use before this RFC was finished.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
Interpreting the data in a data URL carries the same security considerations as any implementation of the given media type. An application should not interpret a data URL marked with a media type that its configuration disallows for processing.

Sites that use firewall proxies to block certain media types, such as script languages or types with known security problems, will find it difficult to screen for them when they arrive inside data URLs. They should be aware of the threat and take precautions within their domain. The RFC also says the effect of long data URLs is unknown, and that some software may behave unreasonably when data exceeds its allocated buffer size.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the content is inside the address, guards that usually check files by type have a harder time seeing what is hidden inside. The content is still as risky as any file of that type.
